memory_update.text: For AI, use hyperscalers, GPU vendors, custom ASIC vendors, and foundries as demand anchors, but map bottleneck research below them into packaging, substrates, HBM test, photonics, power, and qualification gates.
Highest-priority Layer 2A bottleneck candidates: advanced packaging capacity, ABF substrates/materials, HBM-related test/probe/inspection, photonics/InP capacity, and data-center power transformers.

Low-attention supplier lanes to preserve for later layers: inspection/metrology, probe cards, thermal test handlers, OSAT overflow, advanced packaging bonding tools, MOCVD epitaxy, III-V etch/deposition, and qualified transformer suppliers.

Most important catalyst class is hard customer evidence: long-term supply agreements, capacity reservations, customer advance payments, qualification wins, AI/HPC backlog, or explicit HBM/advanced-packaging/optical-interconnect revenue commentary.

Need primary-source verification from company filings and earnings calls for each underfollowed candidate before any company survives Layer 2B: revenue mix, customer concentration, backlog, capacity, lead times, qualification status, and gross-margin impact.
Power-equipment AI exposure needs careful separation between generic electrification/grid demand and AI-specific data-center demand; qualified supplier lists and backlog attribution are required.
CPO and III-V-on-silicon names should remain hypotheses unless supported by customer contracts, production qualification, shipment volumes, or credible capacity reservation evidence.

COHU should remain a high-priority underfollowed AI test candidate mapped to thermal test, high-socket-force handling, inspection/metrology, interface solutions, and HBM inspection; next gate is evidence of repeat AI/HPC platform adoption across multiple customers.

FORM should remain an underfollowed AI test-hardware candidate mapped to HBM probe cards, logic/foundry probe cards, advanced package test, and possible silicon-photonics test; next gate is evidence that HBM probe demand is supply constrained and structurally durable.

AMKR should be treated as a reference advanced-packaging and OSAT capacity candidate rather than a clean underfollowed small/mid-cap; next gate is durable AI/HPC revenue conversion from high-density fan-out, advanced test, and Arizona capacity.

6239.TW should remain a hypothesis-stage underfollowed OSAT candidate tied to memory backend crowding-out, fan-out panel-level packaging, AI/HPC packaging overflow, and possible CPO exposure; primary-source validation is required.
KLIC should remain a hypothesis-stage advanced-packaging equipment candidate; verify whether HBM-related tools and advanced solutions are material enough to offset legacy wire-bond cyclicality.
AIXA.DE should remain a hypothesis-stage upstream AI photonics equipment candidate mapped to MOCVD/epitaxy for III-V photonics and CPO; verify AI optical-interconnect-specific backlog and lead times.

ALMU should remain a speculative shadow candidate only; evidence must confirm commercial readiness, customer contracts, production qualification, revenue scale, and balance-sheet runway before it can graduate.

summary: Split Layer 2 synthesis. Industry-chain map for AI infrastructure using Serenity chokepoint framing: the obvious demand nodes are hyperscalers, GPUs, custom accelerators, and cloud data centers, but the more interesting Layer 2A nodes are constraint layers beneath them: advanced packaging, ABF substrates, HBM/test/probe, OSAT overflow, photonics/InP/CPO, compound-semiconductor process tools, data-center power transformers, and qualification/certification gates. Mega-cap leaders should be treated as demand anchors and validation signals, not the only investable map. Low-attention bottleneck value may hide in niche inspection/metrology, probe cards, thermal test handlers, advanced-packaging equipment, substrate materials, OSAT capacity, III-V photonics tools, and qualified power-equipment suppliers.

supply_chain_map.node: Hyperscaler AI capex and custom accelerator demand
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Cloud providers and large AI customers drive demand for GPUs, custom ASICs, networking, storage, power, and data-center capacity. They are the first-order demand anchors that validate the entire chain, but they are high-attention nodes and should not dominate the bottleneck search.

supply_chain_map.node: GPU and custom AI accelerator design wins
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI training and inference demand translates into NVIDIA GPUs, custom AI accelerators, networking ASICs, and related silicon. The key Serenity question is not only who designs the chips, but which physical layers must scale for those chips to ship.

supply_chain_map.node: Leading-edge foundry wafer capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI accelerators depend on leading-edge foundry capacity. This is a major constraint, but the most visible foundry leaders are already high-attention; they should be used as reference signals for downstream and upstream constraints.

supply_chain_map.node: Advanced packaging capacity: CoWoS, fan-out, hybrid bonding, high-density integration
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI chips require dense die-to-die integration, HBM attachment, interposers, and advanced package test. If advanced-packaging capacity is tight, overflow can benefit OSATs, equipment suppliers, inspection/metrology vendors, and substrate suppliers.

supply_chain_map.node: ABF substrates and high-end package substrates
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Each AI chip generation can require larger, more complex substrates with finer features and more layers. Supplier qualification is long, yields are difficult, and substrate material allocation can reinforce incumbent advantage.

supply_chain_map.node: ABF film and substrate materials
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Advanced substrate makers depend on specialized materials such as ABF film. A scarce upstream material can structure the economics of the substrate bottleneck even when the material supplier itself is not a clean public-market expression.

supply_chain_map.node: HBM supply and HBM-related backend capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI accelerators require HBM stacks and related backend capacity. Bottlenecks can appear not only at memory manufacturers but also in probe cards, inspection, test handling, advanced packaging, and backend outsourcing.

supply_chain_map.node: Semiconductor inspection and metrology for HBM and advanced packaging
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: As packages become larger, denser, and more heterogeneous, yield control becomes more valuable. Low-attention value may hide in inspection and metrology suppliers that screen as cyclical equipment companies but are tied to AI package yield.

supply_chain_map.node: Probe cards and wafer-level test for HBM, logic, and advanced packages
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Higher test intensity and HBM probe-card demand can create bottleneck-adjacent demand for specialized test hardware before AI packages can scale at yield.

supply_chain_map.node: Thermal test, high-socket-force handlers, and AI/HPC test cells
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI processors are large, hot, and power-dense. Test automation, thermal control, and handlers can become practical capacity constraints if AI/HPC platforms require more complex and longer test flows.

supply_chain_map.node: OSAT advanced packaging and test overflow
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: If internal foundry packaging capacity remains tight, outsourced semiconductor assembly and test providers with advanced packaging, fan-out, and high-density package test capabilities may absorb overflow. The key evidence is utilization, customer qualification, and AI/HPC revenue mix.

supply_chain_map.node: Advanced packaging equipment: bonding, thermocompression, vertical wire, wafer-level tools
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI/HPC packages require more complex assembly processes. Tool suppliers can be overlooked when classified under mature bonding cycles, but may benefit if advanced-packaging tool demand becomes visible.

supply_chain_map.node: Optical interconnects for AI data centers
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Scaling AI clusters increases pressure on high-speed optical connectivity. This creates demand for optical modules, lasers, photodetectors, InP devices, and eventually co-packaged optics.

supply_chain_map.node: InP and III-V photonics capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI optical interconnect demand may tighten InP and III-V device capacity. Public-market bottleneck value may hide upstream in photonics materials, epitaxy, etch/deposition tools, and alternative III-V-on-silicon approaches.

supply_chain_map.node: Compound semiconductor epitaxy equipment: MOCVD and related reactors
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Photonics, CPO, and III-V device manufacturing depend on specialized epitaxy tools. These suppliers may be misclassified as broad compound-semiconductor cycle names rather than AI optical-interconnect enablers.

supply_chain_map.node: III-V etch, deposition, and photonics process tools
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: CPO and AI photonics manufacturing require specialized etch/deposition process control. Niche scientific and semiconductor process-tool vendors may be underfollowed due to mixed end-market labels.

supply_chain_map.node: Co-packaged optics development and qualification
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: CPO could shift optical interconnect architecture and create new manufacturing constraints across photonics devices, substrates, packaging, test, and thermal management. Current exposure should be treated as hypothesis unless backed by customer qualification or revenue.

supply_chain_map.node: Data-center power equipment: transformers, switchgear, grid interconnect
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI data centers require large amounts of reliable power. Qualified transformer supply can have multi-year lead times and limited approved suppliers, making it a non-semiconductor bottleneck that constrains AI buildout.

supply_chain_map.node: Qualified supplier lists and customer certification gates
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Long qualification cycles, customer-specific process validation, and approved vendor lists can make capacity hard to replicate even when technology is understood. This is where low-attention value often hides.

supply_chain_map.node: Distributors and allocation channels for scarce components
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: When materials, substrates, optics, or power equipment are scarce, allocation relationships and priority access can matter as much as nominal capacity. This layer is often under-modeled in simple AI stock screens.
